Music City's own

For 26 years, Nashville had its own much-loved theme park.

2.5 million visitors at peak

Opryland USA opened in 1972 and beat every attendance projection in its first season.

26 consecutive years at #1

Nashville's number one tourist attraction for every one of the 26 years it operated.

A showpark and platform for talent

120 acres, 27 attractions and six coasters, built around family entertainment and live American music from local artists.

2M+ visitors a year at its peak — Opryland USA was Music City's Disneyland, and the city has never stopped missing it.

Sources: operating-era estimates; Belcourt Theatre; published accounts of the 1997 season; public record.

The gap in the market

Then, in 1997, it was gone.

The demand for Opryland never left, and the people of Nashville have never stopped missing it or arguing about it.

Nothing has yet been built to meet the inherent market demand for quality family entertainment in this globally famous city.

16.9M

annual visitors to Nashville today, with 20.3M forecast by 2032 — and not a single gated theme park to greet them.

Opryland wasn't closed because crowds stopped coming; the park had peak attendance and profitability in its final year. Today Nashvillians have a mall instead of a theme park, and must drive four hours to the nearest quality park (Dollywood).

Source: Robinett Economics.

Demand history, 1997 to 2026

Opryland was profitable when it closed. Nashville has wanted it back ever since.

1997

Gaylord announced the closure. Within two weeks residents were asking the city to buy the park; the mayor's office replied that preserving it was virtually impossible.

Nashville Scene
2012

A petition to reopen Opryland proposed a new site across the river from Opry Mills.

Change.org
2019

A second petition revived the first, eight years later. Similar campaigns have appeared roughly every decade since the closure.

Change.org
2022

On the 25th anniversary one Opryland Facebook group had more than 21,000 members; a second page had about 10,900 followers.

NewsChannel 5
2025–26

The documentary A Circle Broken screened at the Nashville Film Festival, the Belcourt and the Franklin Theatre. Audiences paid for tickets 29 years on.

Belcourt & Franklin listings
“Opryland was successful. We weren't losing money.”

Bud Wendell · Gaylord CEO, 1974–1997 · WPLN, Curious Nashville

Gaylord closed Opryland to earn a higher return on the land, not because demand had fallen away.

A long and consistent record of public interest, sustained for twenty-eight years with no park to visit — demand for a family theme park in Nashville is already established rather than something the project would have to create.

Sources: Nashville Scene (Dec 2022); WPLN, Curious Nashville; Change.org (2012, 2019); NewsChannel 5 (Dec 2022); Belcourt Theatre and Franklin Theatre listings, 2025–26; Nashville Film Festival 2025. Attendance figures are historical estimates from the operating era. Community membership counts are as reported on the dates shown and have not been independently audited. These figures illustrate public interest; they are not inputs to the attendance forecast.

Attendance methodology

An independent, conservative baseline, benchmarked against 19 comparable parks.

01

Available market

13.3M reachable by 2032: 4.6M residents within two hours and 8.8M overnight leisure visitors.

02

Penetration rates

Residents convert at 15–34% by drive time. Tourists convert at 3.5–5.5%.

03

Benchmark test

Rates checked against 19 named US regional parks: resident penetration 13–34%, averaging 23%.

04

Result

1.50M stabilised visits, in a range of 1.35M to 1.66M. Roughly 75% resident and 25% tourist.

Why the baseline is conservative

  • 1.50M sits below the 19-park comparable median of 1.7M.
  • Assumed resident penetration sits within the comparable range, not above it.
  • Tourist penetration of 3.5–5.5% is set well under the 10% that comparables reach.
  • Prepared by an independent consultant, not by the project team.

Where upside would come from — not in base case

  • Nashville visitor numbers are forecast to grow from 16.9M to 20.3M by 2032, enlarging the tourist pool.
  • The comparable set is unbranded regional parks; national brand awareness is not a variable in the model.
  • No gated theme park competes within a two-hour drive.
  • The base case is presented as modelled; any upside is shown separately as a sensitivity.

Source: Robinett Economics market and feasibility analysis (February 2026 draft), Davidson County lead site, medium case, stabilised year 2032. Figures are modelled projections and are not a forecast or a promise of performance.

Economic projections

$97.9M of revenue and $35.1M of EBITDA at stabilisation, before any of the growth the study left out.

1.50MStabilised visits a yearOpryland averaged about 2M a year in a smaller Nashville

EBITDA Operating costs & reserve

Returns on this case

13.76%All-equity IRR
$66.5MNPV at 10%
2.63xEquity multiple
$291MPeak equity

Not in these numbers

  • No real price increase, ever.Dollywood has taken 1.5–2% a year above inflation for a decade.
  • No new attractions after opening.Only a 5% maintenance reserve; listed operators spend 4–7% more on new rides.
  • No market growth.Nashville visitation is forecast to reach 20.3M by 2032; penetration is held flat.
  • No in-park spend growth.Food and retail per visit are frozen for ten years.

These are the independent study's mid-range figures, not ours. The levers that would move them upward are excluded, not exhausted.
